chem_ocra.14.0.summary: These revision notes explore reversible reactions and the establishment of dynamic equilibrium within closed systems for OCR GCSE Chemistry C5.3. They cover the fundamental differences between forward and reverse rates, the macroscopic properties of equilibrium mixtures, and the conditions necessary to maintain a constant ratio of reactants to products. Mastering these principles allows chemists to understand how industrial processes balance yield and reaction speed.

core.p: A **reversible reaction** is a chemical reaction in which the products can react to reform the original reactants. Unlike reactions that go to completion and use up all limiting reagents, these processes occur in both directions simultaneously under the right conditions.
bullets: Represented in chemical equations using a double half-arrow sign (⇌).
The reaction going from left to right is termed the **forward reaction**.
The reaction going from right to left is termed the **reverse reaction**.
If a reaction is exothermic in one direction, it is endothermic by the exact same energy value in the reverse direction.

callouts.p: A reaction in which the conversion of reactants into products and the conversion of products into reactants occur simultaneously.

core.p: When a reversible reaction takes place in a **closed system**, it eventually reaches a state known as **dynamic equilibrium**. At this stage, macroscopic properties such as concentration, colour, and pressure remain completely constant because the microscopic processes balance out.
bullets: The word **dynamic** means the reactions do not stop; both forward and reverse processes continue actively.
The word **equilibrium** means the opposing rates are perfectly balanced.
No overall change in the amounts of reactants and products is observed outwardly.
Equilibrium can only be achieved inside a closed system where no matter can enter or escape.

callouts.p: Gases or volatile liquids will escape an open container, meaning the reverse reaction cannot occur and equilibrium is never established.

core.p: Two strict conditions must be met simultaneously for any chemical system to maintain dynamic equilibrium. Understanding these conditions helps explain why certain setups fail to establish stable balances.
bullets: 1. The rate of the **forward reaction** must equal the rate of the **reverse reaction**.
2. The system must be a **closed system**, meaning energy can be exchanged with the surroundings, but matter cannot.
Concentrations of all reactants and products remain constant (though not necessarily equal to each other).
Temperature and pressure must also remain constant throughout the system.

callouts.p: Students often wrongly assume that at equilibrium the concentrations of reactants and products are equal. Only their *rates* of reaction are equal.

core.p: In the initial stages of a reversible reaction, reactants are consumed rapidly, so the forward rate is at its maximum. As products form, the reverse rate increases. Equilibrium is reached when these two opposing rates meet and level off at the exact same value.
bullets: Initially: Forward rate is high; reverse rate is zero because no products exist yet.
During transition: Forward rate decreases as reactants are used up; reverse rate increases as products accumulate.
At equilibrium: Rate of forward reaction = Rate of reverse reaction.
Graphically, this is shown where the rate curves for forward and reverse processes flatten out and merge.

core.p: Concentration-time graphs illustrate how amounts change from the start of a reaction until equilibrium is established. The concentration lines curve and eventually become horizontal lines parallel to the time axis.
bullets: Reactant concentrations start high and decrease over time, then level off.
Product concentrations start at zero (in most cases) and increase over time, then level off.
Once horizontal, the concentrations do not change, proving the system has reached equilibrium.
The height of the flat lines depends on the position of equilibrium for that specific reaction.

core.h: Example 1: The Hydrated Copper(II) Sulfate System
core.p: A classic lab demonstration of a reversible reaction involves the thermal decomposition of blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate crystals into white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate and water.
bullets: Equation: CuSO4.5H2O(s) ⇌ CuSO4(s) + 5H2O(l)
Forward reaction: Heating blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate drives off water vapour, leaving white anhydrous powder (Endothermic).
Reverse reaction: Adding liquid water back to white anhydrous copper(II) sulfate produces blue crystals and releases a significant amount of heat (Exothermic).
This system demonstrates a clear colour change between blue and white.

callouts.p: If the forward reaction absorbs thermal energy (endothermic), the reverse reaction must release the exact same quantity of thermal energy (exothermic).

core.h: Example 2: The Haber Process (Nitrogen and Hydrogen)
core.p: The Haber process manufactures ammonia industrially from nitrogen and hydrogen gases. This is a crucial reversible gas-phase reaction used worldwide to produce agricultural fertilizers.
bullets: Equation: N2(g) + 3H2(g) ⇌ 2NH3(g) (+ heat)
Nitrogen is obtained from fractional distillation of liquid air.
Hydrogen is obtained mainly from reacting natural gas (methane) with steam.
The reaction is reversible, meaning unreacted nitrogen and hydrogen gases are recycled continuously through the reaction vessel.

core.h: Example 3: Thermal Decomposition of Ammonium Chloride
core.p: Ammonium chloride is a white solid that decomposes upon heating into two colourless gases: ammonia and hydrogen chloride. When these gases cool down in a cooler part of the test tube, they recombine to form solid ammonium chloride.
bullets: Equation: NH4Cl(s) ⇌ NH3(g) + HCl(g)
Heating takes place at the bottom of the test tube, producing ammonia and hydrogen chloride gases.
As the gases rise and hit cooler glass near the top, they react together to deposit white solid ammonium chloride crystals again.
This is an excellent demonstration of a reversible reaction occurring inside a closed test tube.

core.p: The **position of equilibrium** refers to the relative amounts of reactants and products present in an equilibrium mixture. It indicates whether the mixture contains a higher proportion of reactants or products.
bullets: If the equilibrium lies **to the left**, the mixture contains a higher concentration of reactants.
If the equilibrium lies **to the right**, the mixture contains a higher concentration of products.
Changing reaction conditions (temperature, pressure, concentration) can shift this position.
A catalyst does *not* change the position of equilibrium; it only helps the system reach equilibrium faster.

callouts.p: Always state whether the position of equilibrium shifts 'to the left' or 'to the right' rather than saying the reaction moves.

core.h: The Role of Catalysts in Reversible Reactions
core.p: Adding a catalyst to a reversible reaction speeds up both the forward and the reverse reactions by the exact same proportion. Consequently, it has no effect on the final position of equilibrium.
bullets: Provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower activation energy.
Helps the system reach dynamic equilibrium much more quickly.
Saves industrial manufacturing costs by allowing lower operating temperatures without sacrificing reaction speed.
Does not get used up during the process.

analogy.p: Imagine two people on two side-by-side escalators in a busy department store. One escalator moves upward (representing the forward reaction) and the other moves downward (representing the reverse reaction). People step off the top of the upward escalator and immediately walk over to catch the downward escalator, and vice versa. If people swap escalators at a steady, matching rate, the total number of people on each floor remains completely constant, even though individual people are constantly moving up and down. This represents dynamic equilibrium. Where the analogy breaks down is that chemical particles do not make conscious choices; their movement rates are governed purely by temperature, pressure, and concentration.

terms.d: A reaction in which products can react to form the original reactants.
A state where the rates of the forward and reverse reactions are equal in a closed system, resulting in constant macroscopic properties.
A system isolated from its surroundings so that no matter can enter or leave.
The reaction that produces products from reactants (moving left to right).
The reaction that regenerates reactants from products (moving right to left).
The relative amounts of reactants and products present in a system at dynamic equilibrium.
Containing chemically bound water molecules within its crystalline structure.
A substance containing no water molecules.
The breakdown of a compound into simpler substances using heat.
Large-scale observable characteristics such as colour, pressure, and overall concentration.
The industrial manufacture of ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen gases.
A substance that increases reaction rate without being consumed, by lowering activation energy.

mistakes.w: Saying the reactions stop when equilibrium is reached.
mistakes.r: Reactions are dynamic and continue indefinitely at equal rates in both directions.

mistakes.w: Stating that reactant and product concentrations are equal at equilibrium.
mistakes.r: Only the rates of the forward and reverse reactions are equal; concentrations remain constant but can be unequal.

mistakes.w: Forgetting that a closed system is required for equilibrium.
mistakes.r: Gases will escape an open container, stopping the reverse reaction from occurring.

mistakes.w: Believing a catalyst changes the position of equilibrium.
mistakes.r: A catalyst speeds up both forward and reverse rates equally, leaving the equilibrium position unchanged.

mistakes.w: Writing a single arrow (→) for reversible reactions.
mistakes.r: You must use the double half-arrow symbol (⇌).

mistakes.w: Confusing anhydrous and hydrated copper sulfate colours.
mistakes.r: Hydrated is blue; anhydrous is white.

exam.q: What is meant by the term 'reversible reaction'?
model: A reaction where reactants form products
And products can react to form the original reactants
exam.tip: Make sure to mention both directions of the reaction clearly.

exam.q: Explain what happens to the rate of the forward reaction and the rate of the reverse reaction as a reversible reaction approaches dynamic equilibrium in a closed system.
model: Forward reaction rate decreases over time
Reverse reaction rate increases over time
Eventually, the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction
exam.tip: Link the changes in rates directly to the establishment of equilibrium.

exam.q: Why must a system be closed for dynamic equilibrium to be established?
model: To prevent reactants or products from escaping
So that the reverse reaction can take place
exam.tip: Mention containment of gases or volatile substances to secure full marks.

exam.q: State two features of a reaction system that is in dynamic equilibrium.
model: Rate of forward reaction equals rate of reverse reaction
Concentrations of reactants and products remain constant
exam.tip: Do not state that concentrations are equal; state that they are constant.

exam.q: Describe the colour change observed when water is added to anhydrous copper(II) sulfate.
exam.tip: State both start and end colours clearly.

exam.q: Explain the effect of adding a catalyst on the position of dynamic equilibrium.
model: No effect on the position of equilibrium
Because it speeds up the forward and reverse reactions by the same amount
exam.tip: Always state that catalysts do not shift equilibrium position.

exam.q: Write a balanced symbol equation for the thermal decomposition of ammonium chloride, including state symbols.
exam.tip: Check state symbols carefully: solid reactant yielding two gaseous products.

exam.q: Describe what happens to the macroscopic properties of a system once dynamic equilibrium is reached.
model: Macroscopic properties such as colour and pressure remain constant
Because amounts of substances are no longer changing
exam.tip: Use the term macroscopic properties or give specific examples like colour.

worked.q: A student heats blue hydrated copper(II) sulfate in an open test tube. Explain why the reverse reaction cannot occur until the test tube is sealed or water is added.
steps: Identify that heating hydrated copper sulfate releases water vapour.
Recognize that an open test tube allows water vapour to escape into the room.
Conclude that because water escapes, it is no longer present to react with the anhydrous copper sulfate, preventing the reverse reaction.
worked.ans: The water vapour escapes into the air from the open test tube, meaning it is not a closed system. Without water present, the reverse reaction cannot take place.

worked.q: A gaseous reversible reaction reaches dynamic equilibrium. The forward rate is 0.05 mol/dm³/s. What is the rate of the reverse reaction?
steps: Recall the definition of dynamic equilibrium.
Identify that at equilibrium, the rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction.
State the numerical value of the reverse rate based on this principle.
worked.ans: The rate of the reverse reaction is 0.05 mol/dm³/s because opposing rates are equal at dynamic equilibrium.
